opus-5.5.text:
I think of it as two layers that need to meet in the middle. At the bottom you have skills, things like walking, climbing stairs, picking something up, opening a door. In our world those are mostly learned with reinforcement learning in simulation, and they're very good at the low-level, reactive, contact-rich control that you can't really reason your way through. You don't want a language model deciding where to put each foot at 50 hertz.

But those skills on their own are kind of dumb. They don't know *why* they're doing something or what should come next. That's where the VLM comes in. It has seen an enormous amount of the world through images and text, so it has common sense: if you ask it to clean up a room, it understands that the cup goes to the kitchen, that you probably need to open the drawer before putting something in it, and that if the door is closed you should deal with that first. That kind of semantic, long-horizon reasoning is exactly what the low-level controllers lack.

So the VLM's reasoning ability directly limits how well it can orchestrate. A model that can look at a scene, break a task into steps, pick the right skill with the right parameters, and, importantly, notice when something went wrong and replan, will get much more out of the same set of skills. In practice, a lot of failures aren't the skill failing. They come from the high-level model misreading the scene, picking the wrong order, or not recognizing that a step didn't succeed.

That said, reasoning alone isn't enough. The VLM also needs to understand what the robot is physically capable of. It's easy for a model to propose a plan that looks sensible in language but is infeasible for the body you have. So the interface between the two matters a lot: how you describe the skills to the model, what feedback you give it, how much spatial grounding it has. I see the skills as a vocabulary and the VLM as the thing that composes sentences from it. The richer and more reliable the vocabulary, and the better the model's grasp of both the world and the robot, the more useful behavior you get out of the whole system.

Longer term, I expect that boundary to blur. Some of the reasoning will move down into the policies and some of the physical understanding will move up into the models. For now, though, this split lets each part do what it's good at.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the key thing to understand is that these are really two different problems, and the VLM is only good at one of them. The low-level skills, locomotion over rough terrain, balancing, recovering from a push, manipulating an object with the right contact forces, those are things we train with reinforcement learning in simulation at very high rates, hundreds of hertz, and they don't involve any language or semantic reasoning at all. They're reflexes, essentially. The VLM, on the other hand, operates at a completely different timescale. It sees an image, it reads an instruction, and it reasons about what should happen next in terms of the semantics of the scene, this is a door, there's a box behind it, I should probably go around rather than through.

So the way I think about the relationship is that the VLM's reasoning gives you the ability to compose skills in situations you never explicitly trained for. If you have a library of robust skills and the model understands roughly what each skill does and when it's appropriate, then the generalization you get from the language and vision pretraining transfers into the robot's behavior, even though the model never touched a joint torque. That's the exciting part. The model knows a lot about the world, and the skills become the vocabulary it uses to act in it.

But there's a catch, which is that the reasoning is only as useful as the interface between the two layers. If the skills are brittle, or if the VLM's abstraction of what a skill does doesn't match what it actually does physically, you get these failures where the plan is perfectly sensible on paper and the robot falls over. So a lot of the work is really in designing that interface. How much do you expose? Do you give the model discrete skill calls, or continuous parameters like a target velocity or a goal pose? How does feedback get back up when a skill fails? In my experience, the VLM's reasoning is impressive, but it's also quite naive about physics and timing, and the robustness of the low-level controller is what lets you get away with that naivety. The two capabilities are complementary, and I'd say neither one is close to replacing the other yet.

astra-6.text:
I think of those as two different levels of the problem. The VLM can reason about what needs to happen to accomplish a task, while the robot’s skills handle how to physically execute each step. If you ask a robot to clear a table, the VLM might identify the objects, decide where they belong, and choose which skill to invoke next. It shouldn’t need to generate every motor command.

But being able to describe a sensible plan doesn’t automatically mean it can orchestrate the robot successfully. It needs to understand what the available skills can actually do, when they’re applicable, and whether they succeeded. Then it needs feedback from the world so it can adjust its plan.

So stronger reasoning can help with longer tasks and unexpected situations, but only if it’s grounded in the robot’s capabilities. A very capable planner with unreliable skills will still struggle, and a robot with excellent skills needs something that can put them together appropriately.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of the VLM as operating at a higher level of abstraction. It can look at a scene, interpret what you’re asking for, and reason about which skills to execute and in what order. But that doesn’t automatically mean it can control the robot well. You still need skills that reliably translate those decisions into physical actions.

The two are closely connected, though. To make a useful plan, the model needs some understanding of what each skill can accomplish and under what conditions it will work. And after executing a skill, it needs feedback: Did the robot actually pick up the object? Has the situation changed? Should it try again or choose a different action?

So I wouldn’t equate stronger reasoning with better robotics performance directly. Stronger reasoning can improve the orchestration, but only if it’s grounded in the robot’s capabilities and what’s actually happening in the environment.
